caseNote: 가상 사례 두 개 (도장 업체, 소프트웨어 회사 안의 제품팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 어떤 선택의 진짜 비용은 쓴 돈이 아니라, 그 시간과 자원으로 할 수 있었던 차선책의 가치다.
misconception: 현금이 나가지 않으면 비용이 없다. 원가만 받으면 손해가 아니고, 월급이 어차피 나가는 회의는 공짜다.

sources.text: 경제학 입문의 표준 개념 (기회비용: 포기한 차선책의 가치). 예: Mankiw, Principles of Economics

factChecks.note: 도장 업체 계산: 친구 가게 작업 가격 $1,800 − 페인트·인건비 $1,800 = $0. 포기한 작업 $4,000 − $2,500 = $1,500. 친구 작업의 기회비용 $1,500.
회의 계산: 8명 × 1.5시간 × 시간당 인건비(급여·복리후생 포함 가정) $100 = $1,200/주. × 연 50주 = $60,000. 시간당 $100은 설명용 가정이며, 인건비는 기회비용의 대략적인 대용치일 뿐이라는 점을 카드에 밝혔습니다.
맞춤 기능 사례($20,000, 4주)는 가상 수치이며 비교 대상 기능의 가치는 일부러 수치화하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Your 'free' meeting cost $1,200
body: Eight people sit in a weekly 90-minute meeting. No invoice arrives. Nobody pays a cent extra.
Across town, a painter does a favor for a friend and charges only for paint and wages. It looks like it costs nothing.
Both are expensive. The bill just doesn't show up where anyone looks.

image.label: A meeting room clock and a paint roller, each with an invisible price tag
image.brief: 화면을 좌우로 나눔. 왼쪽은 8명이 앉은 회의실과 벽시계, 오른쪽은 페인트 롤러와 페인트 통. 양쪽 모두 점선으로 된 투명한 가격표가 매달려 있고 가격표에 물음표. 실제 로고·상표 없음.

cards.title: What does the favor really cost?
body: You run a three-person painting crew. A friend asks you to paint his shop next week. You'll charge $1,800, exactly what the paint and wages cost.
That same week, you could take a $4,000 house job that leaves $1,500 after paint and wages. That customer can't wait. What does the favor cost you?

options.text: Nothing. Paint and wages are covered
options.feedback: Your cash balances out, so it feels free. But you gave up the house job, and that loss never appears in your books.

options.text: About $1,500, the profit from the job you turn down
options.feedback: Right. The crew can only be in one place. The real price of the favor is what the crew would have earned elsewhere.

options.text: Only the hours you personally spend on it
options.feedback: Good instinct that time matters. But it's the whole crew's week that's used up, not just yours.

cards.title: One crew, one week, two options.
body: The favor shows $0 profit. Choosing it means giving up **$1,500**. That's the number that belongs on the decision.

breakdown.label: Real cost of the favor
breakdown.detail: The best option you gave up

cards.title: Opportunity cost
body: **Opportunity cost** is the value of the best option you give up when you choose something. It's the road not taken, measured.
Because time, people and money are limited, every yes is a no to something else. The cash you spend is only part of the price.
The painter didn't lose money on paper. He lost the house job.

cards.title: The weekly meeting that nobody pays for.
body: A product team at a software company holds a 90-minute status meeting every week. Eight people attend. With salary and benefits, each person costs the company about $100 an hour.
8 people × 1.5 hours × $100 = **$1,200 a week**, or about $60,000 a year.
And salary is only a rough guide. The true cost is what those eight people would have built, fixed or sold in that time.

image.label: Eight people around a table, a running cost meter on the wall
image.brief: 회의실 벽에 택시 미터기처럼 숫자가 올라가는 카운터가 있고 "$1,200"에서 멈춰 있음. 테이블 위 노트북들은 덮여 있고, 창밖으로 미완성 작업 상자들이 쌓여 있는 느낌. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Opportunity costs never send an invoice.
body: Your books record money that moves. They don't record money you could have earned. So the biggest costs of a choice are often invisible.
Look for it wherever something is limited:
list: **Your own evening** spent on a task someone else could do
**Cash** sitting idle instead of funding a better project
**Shelf or floor space** given to a slow seller

cards.title: The alternative has to be real.
body: Opportunity cost is only as big as your next-best option. If the crew had no other work that week, the favor costs almost nothing and may build goodwill.
The same goes for meetings. One that prevents a month of rework is cheap. Don't time every minute. Ask the question for big or repeated choices, and keep the estimate rough.

cards.title: A customer wants a custom feature.
body: You lead a software team. A large customer offers $20,000 for a custom feature that would take your team four weeks.
What should you compare the $20,000 against?

options.text: The team's salary cost for those four weeks
options.feedback: This tells you whether the cash covers the cost. It doesn't tell you what the team stops building while it works on this.

options.text: The value of what the team would build instead in those four weeks
options.feedback: That's the real trade. If the planned work would keep or win more customers than $20,000 is worth, the deal costs you money.

options.text: Nothing. $20,000 of new revenue beats zero
options.feedback: The alternative is never zero. The team's four weeks would have produced something, and that's what you give up.

cards.title: Every yes has a price: the best thing you said no to.
body: Before calling something free, ask what else the same time, people or money could do.
**Try it today:** pick one recurring meeting or task. Multiply people by hours, then write down one thing that time could produce instead.
